html:
Madagascar was settled by Austronesian seafarers from Southeast Asia, most likely from southern Borneo, roughly in the 5th to 7th centuries CE, and later by people from East Africa. The mix of the two made the Malagasy people.

The clearest evidence is language. Malagasy is an Austronesian language, closely related to the Ma'anyan language of southeastern Borneo, with loanwords from Malay, Javanese and Bantu languages. Genetic studies agree: most Malagasy have both Southeast Asian and African ancestry, in shares that vary across the island.

The voyage was part of the long Austronesian expansion that began when farmers and sailors moved south from Taiwan to the Philippines around 2200 BCE. The same seafaring skill took others east across the Pacific. How the settlers crossed the Indian Ocean is debated: perhaps directly, perhaps in stages along the coasts of India and East Africa. Malay and Javanese traders were active in the Indian Ocean in this period, and Madagascar may have been reached by people working in that trade.

They brought rice, bananas, outrigger canoes and other Southeast Asian ways of life. Rice terraces in the highlands still look like those of Java and the Philippines. Bantu-speaking peoples from the mainland, part of the Bantu expansion, brought cattle and African crops.

Dates are uncertain. There may have been earlier visits, and human activity is clearest from around 500 CE onward. The island's giant lemurs, elephant birds and pygmy hippos died out in the centuries after people arrived. Later contacts with the Swahili coast and Arab traders brought Islam to the north, and from the 18th century the Merina kingdom unified much of the island.
sum: Madagascar was settled by Austronesian seafarers from Southeast Asia, most likely from southern Borneo, roughly in the 5th to 7th centuries CE, and later by people from East Africa. The mix of the two made the Malagasy people.
